hints: Focus on what type of compound must react with both HCN and NaBH4, and remember what a chiral centre really needs.
Recall that HCN adds to the C=O to give a cyanohydrin, while NaBH4 reduces the C=O to an alcohol, so draw the two products for each carbonyl.
Check which starting carbonyl gives four different groups on the new carbon in both products, as symmetry with two identical methyl or two H atoms will destroy chirality.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the functional group in Q**

Q reacts with both HCN and NaBH4. That is classic carbonyl chemistry. HCN undergoes nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins, and NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.

$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C(OH)(CN)}$$ 
$$\text{R}_2\text{C=O} \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{R}_2\text{CH(OH)}$$

**Recall the test for a chiral centre**

A chiral carbon has four different groups attached to it. So after each reaction, look at the carbon that was the C=O carbon and ask, are all four groups different?

Chiral centre condition: $\text{C}$ attached to 4 different substituents.

**Test butanone**

Butanone is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, an unsymmetrical ketone.

With HCN: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
The new centre has $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$. All four different, so chiral.

With NaBH4: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
This is butan-2-ol. C-2 has $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}$. All four different, so chiral. Both conditions are met.

**See why the others fail**

Ethanal and propanal give a chiral cyanohydrin but reduction gives a primary alcohol with no chiral centre. Propanone is symmetrical with two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so both its cyanohydrin and its alcohol have two identical methyl groups and cannot be chiral. Only butanone works for both.

options.A: Butanone is correct. It is unsymmetrical, so addition of HCN gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile with four different groups on C-2, and reduction gives butan-2-ol with four different groups on C-2. Both products contain a chiral centre.
options.B: Ethanal is wrong. With HCN it does give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CN}$ which is chiral, but with NaBH4 it gives ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which has no carbon with four different groups. Students choosing this often check only the HCN reaction.
options.C: Propanal is wrong. With HCN it gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CN}$ which is chiral, but with NaBH4 it gives propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, which is achiral. Like ethanal, it fails the reduction test.
options.D: Propanone is wrong. It is a symmetrical ketone, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=O}$. Its cyanohydrin, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)CN}$, has two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups, and its reduction product, propan-2-ol, also has two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups. Neither product can be chiral.
